newsitem.title: UK: UK watchdog to cast cloud over public finances.
newsitem.headline: UK watchdog to cast cloud over public finances.

text.p: An independent report on Britain's public finances, due for release on Thursday, is likely to conclude the previous government made overly optimistic forecasts about jobs and growth when it drew up the last budget.

City analysts said the National Audit Office(NAO), a government watchdog, is also likely to criticise the practice of factoring in privatisation proceeds to budget calculations before legislation is drawn up.
It is also likely to conclude that plans from the previous government to recoup billions of pounds in tax receipts are unrealistic.
"The report is likely to present a more gloomy medium-term outlook of the public finances than we saw in the budget last November," said Jonathan Loynes, UK economist at HSBC Markets.
"But it isn't likely to find the much-talked of black hole. And in terms of the next two years the chances of a hefty undershoot of the PSBR forecast look extremely good."
On May 20, the new Chancellor of the Exchequer Gordon Brown asked the NAO to review the key assumptions made by the previous government.
Its report will come well before he presents his first budget on July 20, which has led to speculation that he will seek to use its findings to justify tax rises.
The previous Conservative government upped its forecast for economic growth in the medium term to 2.5 percent each year from 1999 onwards from a previous forecast of 2.25 percent.

Former Chancellor Kenneth Clarke also changed the practice of assuming unemployment will stay constant and factored in a continually falling jobless total instead, which implied lower public spending on benefits.

"Clarke assumed that unemployment was falling and would continue to fall. He was right, and in fact unemployment has fallen further than even he thought, but I think the NAO will probably suggest the government reverts back to assuming unchanged unemployment," said Loynes.
The choice of the National Audit Office to carry out the review was criticised by Clarke who said it was an inappropriate body to conduct the review and not geared up to do the job.

Some economists said the NAO's skill in assessing long term growth forecasts may be questionable, but its expertise is accounting means its views on the so-called "spend-to-save" plan and treatment of privatisation proceeds within the budget will carry more weight.
In its November budget, the previous government claimed it could recoup 7.0 billion pounds of tax revenue if it spent 800 million pounds over the next three years clamping down on tax evasion.
"It's quite likely the NAO will say this is far too optimistic," said Michael Dicks, UK economist at Lehman Brothers.
He said the NAO may suggest that evidence based on the success of local schemes should be used to try and estimate the savings on a national level.
"Or it may recommend that nothing is assumed until some substantial savings have already been made, which can be set aside for the future."
A similar scaling back of projections of privatisation proceeds may also be recommended.

There was some criticism at the time of the last budget that the previous government's calculations assumed privatisations would continue to reel in around a billion pounds a year for the forseeable future.

That budget assumed receipts of 2.0 billion pounds this fiscal year, falling to 1.5 billion pounds in 1998/99, falling again to 1.0 billion pounds for each year thereafter. Plans for privatisations in this later period are very thin indeed.

Those projected receipts count as 'negative spending' in the sums, effectively offsetting a portion of departmental spending. So they are crucial to the new government's spending plans, given its commitment to meet tight spending targets for the next two years.
"The audit office may say it is more sensible to keep privatisation proceeds out of the picture until the legislation is drawn up," said Dicks.
